questions.question: Which set of numbers represent the choices of Rock, Paper, and Scissors in our custom game comparison logic?
questions.explanation: Perfect! Representing choices as numbers (1=Rock, 2=Paper, 3=Scissors) simplifies writing comparison checks in Python.

questions.question: Under which set of conditions does the Player win the round against the AI in Rock-Paper-Scissors?
options: When Player has 1 (Rock) & AI has 3 (Scissors), OR Player has 2 (Paper) & AI has 1 (Rock), OR Player has 3 (Scissors) & AI has 2 (Paper)
When Player chooses 1 (Rock) and AI has 2 (Paper)
When Player chooses 3 (Scissors) and AI has 1 (Rock)
questions.explanation: Spot on! Rock (1) beats Scissors (3); Paper (2) beats Rock (1); and Scissors (3) beats Paper (2). These are the three winning paths for the player.

questions.question: Which OpenCV function is used to overlay text, scores, or timers directly onto the video frames?
questions.explanation: Correct! cv2.putText() is the standard method used to overlay text strings on visual matrices, allowing you to define font styles, sizes, and colors.

questions.question: In OpenCV's putText function, what color is represented by the BGR tuple (255, 0, 255)?
options: Magenta / Purple (mixture of Blue and Red)
questions.explanation: Excellent! OpenCV handles colors in Blue-Green-Red (BGR) order. (255, 0, 255) represents a mixture of Blue (255) and Red (255) with Green (0), forming Magenta.

questions.question: Simple Coding Task: Write a Python statement to check if player choice (player = 2) beats AI choice (ai = 1) using 'and', and print the string 'Player wins!'.
questions.task_hint: Write: player = 2 then ai = 1 then if player == 2 and ai == 1: print('Player wins!')
questions.explanation: Outstanding! Conditional assertions correctly decide the round winner based on mapped inputs.
